abstract: |
  Using the daily air-quality readings that ship with R, this note asks how
  much of the day-to-day variation in New York's summer ozone tracks the
  weather. Ozone climbs from May into a July and August peak, and the
  readings above 70 parts per billion cluster in those two months. Hotter,
  calmer days carry markedly more ozone: temperature and wind together
  account for well over half of the variance. The document doubles as the
  docdesigner style specimen, so it carries one of each element a research
  paper uses.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.1, out.width = "100%",
                      fig.align = "center")

# Figures take the style's own colours, so a chart belongs to its page.
pal <- docdesigner::designer_style(params$style)$color
accent <- pal$accent
muted  <- if (is.null(pal$muted)) "#666666" else pal$muted
grid   <- if (is.null(pal$rule)) "#CCCCCC" else pal$rule
par_style <- function() {
  par(mar = c(3.6, 3.8, 0.8, 0.8), mgp = c(2.4, 0.6, 0), tcl = -0.25,
      las = 1, bty = "n", col.axis = muted, col.lab = muted, cex.axis = 0.85)
}

aq <- airquality
aq$month <- factor(month.name[aq$Month], levels = month.name[5:9])
aq$date  <- as.Date(sprintf("1973-%02d-%02d", aq$Month, aq$Day))
std <- 70                                    # ppb, reference line only
aq$high <- aq$Ozone > std

n_days   <- nrow(aq)
n_ozone  <- sum(!is.na(aq$Ozone))
n_high   <- sum(aq$high, na.rm = TRUE)
by_month <- tapply(aq$Ozone, aq$month, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
peak     <- names(which.max(by_month))

m1 <- lm(Ozone ~ Temp, data = aq)
m2 <- lm(Ozone ~ Temp + Wind + Solar.R, data = aq)
b_temp <- coef(m2)[["Temp"]]
b_wind <- coef(m2)[["Wind"]]
r2_1 <- summary(m1)$r.squared
r2_2 <- summary(m2)$r.squared

f1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
```

# Introduction

Ground-level ozone is not emitted directly. It forms when nitrogen oxides and
volatile organic compounds react in sunlight, so its concentration should
follow the weather as much as it follows traffic and industry. Hot, still,
bright afternoons are the textbook recipe. This note checks that recipe
against a small and famous dataset: the `r n_days` daily readings taken in New
York between May and September 1973 and published by @chambers1983, which
have shipped with R ever since [@rcore2025].

The analysis is deliberately simple. It describes the season, counts the days
with high readings, and fits two linear models. Its second purpose is to give
each docdesigner style the same realistic material to set: prose with
citations, figures, three kinds of table, a quotation, code, a highlighted
finding and a reference list [@xie2018].

> The greatest value of a picture is when it forces us to notice what we
> never expected to see.
>
> --- John W. Tukey [-@tukey1977]

# Data

Each row is a day. Ozone is the mean concentration in parts per billion (ppb)
from 1 to 3 pm on Roosevelt Island; solar radiation is measured in Langleys
in Central Park; wind is the average speed in miles per hour at LaGuardia
Airport; and temperature is the daily maximum in degrees Fahrenheit, also at
LaGuardia. Ozone is missing on `r n_days - n_ozone` of the `r n_days` days and
solar radiation on `r sum(is.na(aq$Solar.R))`; the models below drop those
days. Table 1 summarises the four measures.

```{r stats}
vars <- c(Ozone = "Ozone (ppb)", Solar.R = "Solar radiation (Ly)",
          Wind = "Wind (mph)", Temp = "Maximum temperature (°F)")
stats <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(vars), function(v) {
  x <- aq[[v]]
  data.frame(Measure = vars[[v]], N = sum(!is.na(x)),
             Mean = f1(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)), SD = f1(sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
             Min = f1(min(x, na.rm = TRUE)), Median = f1(median(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
             Max = f1(max(x, na.rm = TRUE)))
}))
knitr::kable(stats, format = "pipe", row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrr",
             caption = "Daily measures, New York, May to September 1973")
```

As a reference point the figures and tables use 70 ppb, the level of the
current federal ozone standard [@epa2015]. That standard applies to an
eight-hour average, not a two-hour afternoon mean, so the line marks unusually
high readings; it is not a test of compliance.

# Results

## The season

Ozone builds through the summer. Figure 1 traces the daily
readings; the gaps are missing days. The highest values arrive in late July
and August, and May and September are comparatively clean.

```{r line, fig.cap = "Daily afternoon ozone, May to September 1973. The dashed line marks 70 ppb."}
par_style()
plot(aq$date, aq$Ozone, type = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "Ozone (ppb)",
     ylim = c(0, max(aq$Ozone, na.rm = TRUE)))
abline(h = pretty(c(0, 170)), col = grid, lwd = 0.5)
abline(h = std, col = muted, lty = 2, lwd = 1)
lines(aq$date, aq$Ozone, col = accent, lwd = 1.4)
points(aq$date, aq$Ozone, col = accent, pch = 16, cex = 0.35)
```

Averaged by month (Figure 2), the pattern is plainer. Mean ozone
in `r peak` is `r f1(max(by_month))` ppb, roughly
`r f1(max(by_month) / by_month[["May"]])` times the May mean of
`r f1(by_month[["May"]])` ppb.

```{r bar, fig.cap = "Mean afternoon ozone by month."}
par_style()
mids <- barplot(by_month, col = accent, border = NA, ylab = "Mean ozone (ppb)",
                ylim = c(0, max(by_month) * 1.18), names.arg = month.abb[5:9],
                space = 0.45)
text(mids, by_month, f1(by_month), pos = 3, cex = 0.8, col = muted)
```

Means hide spread. The box plots in Figure 3 show that July and
August are not just higher on average but far more variable, with a long
upper tail: the summer's worst days are much worse than its typical ones.

```{r box, fig.cap = "Distribution of daily ozone by month. Boxes span the middle half of days; the line inside is the median."}
par_style()
boxplot(Ozone ~ month, data = aq, names = month.abb[5:9], xlab = "",
        ylab = "Ozone (ppb)", col = adjustcolor(accent, alpha.f = 0.25),
        border = accent, medcol = accent, whiskcol = accent, staplecol = accent,
        outcol = accent, outpch = 16, outcex = 0.5, boxwex = 0.55, frame = FALSE)
abline(h = std, col = muted, lty = 2, lwd = 1)
```

## High-ozone days

Table 2 cross-tabulates month against whether the day's reading
exceeded 70 ppb. Of the `r n_ozone` days with a reading, `r n_high`
(`r round(100 * n_high / n_ozone)`%) were above the line, and July and August
supply most of them.

```{r xtab}
tab <- table(aq$month, factor(aq$high, c(FALSE, TRUE), c("No", "Yes")))
pct <- 100 * tab[, "Yes"] / rowSums(tab)
xt <- data.frame(Month = rownames(tab),
                 `70 ppb or below` = as.integer(tab[, "No"]),
                 `Above 70 ppb` = as.integer(tab[, "Yes"]),
                 `Share above` = paste0(round(pct), "%"),
                 check.names = FALSE)
xt <- rbind(xt, data.frame(Month = "All months",
                           `70 ppb or below` = sum(tab[, "No"]),
                           `Above 70 ppb` = sum(tab[, "Yes"]),
                           `Share above` = paste0(round(100 * n_high / n_ozone), "%"),
                           check.names = FALSE))
knitr::kable(xt, format = "pipe", row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrr",
             caption = "Days above 70 ppb by month (days with an ozone reading)")
```

## Weather and ozone

The models are ordinary least squares, fitted in R as below. Model 1 uses
temperature alone; Model 2 adds wind speed and solar radiation.

```{r models, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
m1 <- lm(Ozone ~ Temp, data = airquality)
m2 <- lm(Ozone ~ Temp + Wind + Solar.R, data = airquality)
summary(m2)
```

```{r reg}
stars <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "***", ifelse(p < .01, "**", ifelse(p < .05, "*", "")))
cell <- function(m, term) {
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  if (!term %in% rownames(co)) return(c("", ""))
  c(paste0(f2(co[term, 1]), stars(co[term, 4])), paste0("(", f2(co[term, 2]), ")"))
}
terms <- c(Temp = "Maximum temperature (°F)", Wind = "Wind (mph)",
           Solar.R = "Solar radiation (Ly)", `(Intercept)` = "Constant")
rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(terms), function(t) {
  a <- cell(m1, t); b <- cell(m2, t)
  data.frame(Term = c(terms[[t]], ""), `Model 1` = a, `Model 2` = b, check.names = FALSE)
}))
rows <- rbind(rows,
  data.frame(Term = c("Observations", "R²"),
             `Model 1` = c(nobs(m1), f2(r2_1)),
             `Model 2` = c(nobs(m2), f2(r2_2)), check.names = FALSE))
knitr::kable(rows, format = "pipe", row.names = FALSE, align = "lrr",
             caption = "OLS models of daily ozone (ppb). Standard errors in parentheses; \\* p < .05, \\*\\* p < .01, \\*\\*\\* p < .001")
```

Temperature alone accounts for `r round(100 * r2_1)`% of the variance in daily
ozone (Table 3). Adding wind and sunlight raises that to
`r round(100 * r2_2)`%. Holding the other two constant, each additional degree
of maximum temperature goes with `r f2(b_temp)` ppb more ozone, and each
additional mile per hour of wind with `r f2(abs(b_wind))` ppb less: wind
disperses what heat and sunlight produce.

::: {.callout title="Key finding"}
On the hottest, calmest days of 1973 New York's afternoon ozone ran far above
its seasonal norm. Each extra degree of maximum temperature added about
`r f1(b_temp)` ppb and each extra mile per hour of wind removed about
`r f1(abs(b_wind))` ppb; together with sunlight, the weather explains
`r round(100 * r2_2)`% of the day-to-day variation.
:::

The relationship is not linear at the extremes, and a model of the logarithm
of ozone fits the upper tail better. For a single season of readings from one
site, though, the simple model makes the point.

# Conclusion

Summer ozone in New York in 1973 tracked the weather closely. The season
peaked in July and August, high readings clustered there, and hot, still days
carried the most ozone.
